newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Wife of U.N. chief seeks her own space in New York.
newsitem.headline: Wife of U.N. chief seeks her own space in New York.

text.p: When Kofi Annan was elected U.N. secretary-general last month his artist wife Nane walked clear across Manhattan to join him at the United Nations, relishing the last moments without bodyguards.

A very private person, trained as a lawyer, the Swedish-born wife of the seventh secretary-general reluctantly gives up her anonymity as she gets ready to live in the U.N. townhouse that will become her home for the next five years.
"I am sure I will find a room of my own," she said, smiling shyly during a recent interview.
She wonders if the guards will come along on hiking trips to Norway, where her brother lives. Long walks in New York, in Sweden, in Norway, in Ghana are a speciality of the couple.

Asked if she would keep up the U.N. tradition of borrowing paintings from museums, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art, she said, "Oh yes, my great uncle's wife was painted by Modigliani in Paris and that is supposed to be at the Met."

The former Nane Lagergren, 52, met her husband, a Ghanaian, in 1981 when they both worked for U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in Geneva. They were married in 1984 at the U.N. Chapel in New York by a women minister, who also painted. It was the second marriage for both.

With a long line of lawyers on both sides of her family -- some of whom were also artists -- Annan said she studied law to "show we (women) were able to have a profession." She worked as an associate judge and legislative counsel in Stockholm, drawing on the side.
In New York she studied at the Art Students League. "I had to train my hands first, and then do abstract painting," she said. "They broke me out of the traditional mode."
She then went to the the New York Studio School, devoted to figurative art, where she worked from "9 in the morning until 10 at night, about the same hours as Kofi."
"Painting at this stage has become an act of meditation," she said. "For me painting is a search. I am interested in painting the human being. That is what life is all about."

Human figures are discernable in her abstract paintings in dark strong colours. She has been teased by some friends about leaning towards "heavy metal" paintings of leaping motorcycles that belie her tall, striking, ladylike appearance.

"Those were the ones in reaction to being a Swedish bureaucrat facing questions of life and death," she said. "When we grew up there was so much hope of more tolerance and understanding in the world. That is not so."
Nane Lagergren is the niece of Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved tens of thousands of Jews in Hungary from the Nazis at the end of World War Two.
His last letter home arrived shortly after Nane was born and before he disappeared, presumably into a Soviet prison, and included the lines, "Kiss the little one for me."
"He was a constant presence, an absence, a shadow," she says of her childhood.

Her jurist father, Gunnar Lagregren, helped settle boundary disputes between India and Pakistan, served on German restitution courts and arbitrated claims between the United States and Iran. Her daughter Nina, 25, is also a lawyer.
Her parents took to Kofi immediately and her mother, she joked, has become the "First Mother-in-Law of Sweden."
Asked if there was a European-African culture gap in their marriage, she said their biggest problem was arriving at dinner parties on time -- she early, he late.
Her promptness has caused her daughter to joke that even if "your best friend invites you half an hour later than the other guests, you are still the first one to arrive."

She described Ghana as warm and welcoming. During the family's recent Christmas holiday there, "about 30 of his classmates came to the house and they were like children, like happy little boys." They were joined by Nina and Kofi's two children Ama, 26, and Kojo, 23.
Unimpressed by the attention she is receiving, Nane Annan (pronounced Nan as in Dan) nevertheless is excited about her husband's new role and proud of his accomplishments.

She recalls that walk from a restaurant on Tenth Avenue to U.N. headquarters on First Avenue on December 13. A woman stopped her, asking if she had attended the 1995 Beijing Women's Conference because she was carrying a U.N. bag.
Annan says she answered "no" and then had the impulse to chase her and shout, "'Well, my husband was just elected secretary-general ... of the United Nations.'"
